answer_text:
Let

\[
W_n(s)=B_{n-1+s}-B_{n-1},\qquad 0\le s\le 1.
\]

By the independent increments property of Brownian motion, the processes \((W_n(s))_{0\le s\le 1}\) are independent copies of a standard Brownian motion on \([0,1]\). Hence

\[
M_n=\max_{n-1\le t\le n}|B_t-B_{n-1}|
=\sup_{0\le s\le 1}|W_n(s)|
\]

and the random variables \(M_n\) are i.i.d., with the same law as

\[
R=\sup_{0\le s\le 1}|W_s|
\]

for a standard Brownian motion \(W\).

We need the large-deviation tail of \(R\). Let \(M^+=\sup_{0\le s\le 1}W_s\). By the reflection principle,

\[
\mathbb P(M^+>x)=2(1-\Phi(x)),\qquad x>0,
\]

where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cdf. Since

\[
R> x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M^+>x \text{ or } \sup_{0\le s\le 1}(-W_s)>x,
\]

we have

\[
\mathbb P(R>x)\le 4(1-\Phi(x)).
\]

Also \(R\ge |W_1|\), so

\[
\mathbb P(R>x)\ge \mathbb P(|W_1|>x)=2(1-\Phi(x)).
\]

Using the standard Gaussian tail estimate

\[
1-\Phi(x)\sim \frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{x\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad x\to\infty,
\]

we obtain

\[
\mathbb P(R>x)\asymp x^{-1}e^{-x^2/2}.
\]

Now fix \(r>0\) and set \(x_n=r\sqrt{\log n}\). Then for large \(n\),

\[
\mathbb P(M_n>r\sqrt{\log n})
\asymp
\frac{n^{-r^2/2}}{\sqrt{\log n}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb P(M_n>r\sqrt{\log n})<\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{r^2}{2}>1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r>\sqrt2.
\]

- If \(r>\sqrt2\), the Borel–Cantelli lemma gives

\[
\mathbb P(M_n>r\sqrt{\log n}\ \text{i.o.})=0,
\]

so with probability one, \(M_n\le r\sqrt{\log n}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

- If \(0<r\le \sqrt2\), the series diverges. Since the events \(\{M_n>r\sqrt{\log n}\}\) are independent, the second Borel–Cantelli lemma gives

\[
\mathbb P(M_n>r\sqrt{\log n}\ \text{i.o.})=1,
\]

so the desired eventual bound fails almost surely.

Thus the sharp threshold is \(\sqrt2\). More precisely, the statement holds almost surely exactly for \(r>\sqrt2\), while it fails for \(r\le\sqrt2\). Hence the critical value is

\[
\boxed{\sqrt{2}}.
\]
